title: Flower 101: Grinding, Rolling, Storing | The Bridge
description: Three basic flower skills with the research behind them: grind later than you think, skip the tobacco wrap, and keep the jar cool, dark and whole.
lede: Three basic skills, and the research has opinions about at least one of them. Grind later than you think, and keep the jar out of the light.
html:
Nobody hands you a manual for this. You learn from a friend on a stoop, and some of what that friend told you was wrong. Holding your breath, for one: New York's own guide says cannabis absorbs almost instantly when inhaled, and holding it in just makes you lightheaded. So here are the basics, with the research where there is some.

Grinding: later than you think

Pull out any stems, give the grinder a few turns and stop while the flower is still fluffy. Then use it. In a 2020 storage study, all of the ground samples held lower terpenoid levels than their whole counterparts after four months, and the authors named grinding among the least favorable conditions for keeping them. A jar of pre-ground flower is convenient. It is also where the smell goes to die.

When you're done, brush out the grinder and put it away with everything else. The state's storage card specifically says to clean up ground flower, crumbs, lighters and matches.

Rolling: practice beats theory

  1. Roll a small strip of thin, plain card into a tight tube for the tip.
  2. Lay the paper flat with the glue strip at the top edge, facing you. Set the tip at one end.
  3. Spread the ground flower evenly along the crease. Use less than you think.
  4. Pinch the paper and roll it back and forth between your thumbs and fingers until it holds a cylinder.
  5. Tuck the bare edge over the flower, roll up and seal the glue strip.
  6. Tap the flower down with a pen and twist the open end closed.

Your first few will look terrible. That's the standard route. If you'd rather skip it, pre-rolls exist for a reason.

Some notes from the state's guide. Blunts and cigar papers contain tobacco, which it says may add negative health effects, and there are plenty of other papers to choose from. Roll your own instead of passing one around, since sharing can spread illness. Take one or two puffs and wait five to ten minutes before deciding on more. And the state is plain about smoke: like tobacco smoke, it contains tar and cancer-causing chemicals, so keep it away from other people.

Where you light it matters too. Adults 21 and over can generally consume in a private home or most places tobacco is allowed. Not in a vehicle, on a restaurant patio, in a hookah or cigar bar, in a public park or on federal property. Landlords can ban smoking on their premises, so read your lease.

Storing: cool, dark, whole

The guide warns that flower left out or exposed to light and air can get moldy. Temperature matters as well. The 2020 study found 25°C, about room temperature, caused the largest changes in cannabinoids over a year, and that whole flower at 4°C, refrigerator temperature, held up best overall. A 2026 University of Mississippi study found room temperature sped up THC's breakdown into CBN, and that a freezer at minus 20°C best preserved potency.

Terpenes complicate the picture. The 2020 team found temperatures colder than minus 20°C among the worst conditions for them. So colder isn't automatically smarter, and what keeps the THC may not keep the smell.

For most people that adds up to something simple. Keep flower whole until you need it, sealed, somewhere dark and cool, and buy an amount you'll finish before it fades. Keep it in the original package, because that label carries the warnings and the THC content. And lock it up. Safe storage at home gets its own page, because it matters more than anything else on this one.
